background.definition: Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve characterized by subacute monocular or binocular vision loss over days to weeks, periorbital pain associated with eye movement, and loss of color vision. It is often the initial manifestation of multiple sclerosis. If associated with myelitis of the spinal nerves, it is called neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, an entity distinct from MS, also known as Devic's disease. This represents 1-3% of patients with acute optic neuritis.

list.listitem: Optic neuritis typically occurs in patients between the ages of 20 and 45 years with a mean age of 32 years.
Seventy-seven percent of patients are female.
Northern Europeans are 8 times more likely to have optic neuritis than Blacks or Asians.
In Europe, the incidence is 5 cases per 100,000 persons/year.
Optic neuritis is often the initial manifestation of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Multiple sclerosis
Idiopathic
Lyme disease, tuberculosis, syphilis
HIV, hepatitis B, cytomegalovirus, herpes
Contiguous inflammation of the orbit, sinuses, or meninges
Drugs (ethambutol, interferon-α, infliximab, pembrolizumab, and other tumor necrosis factor inhibitors).
Vasculitis
Inflammation of the optic nerve may occur secondary to infection, medication toxicity, or demyelination.

In patients with multiple sclerosis, the lesions in the optic nerve are similar to those seen in the brain, with an inflammatory response characterized by the presence of plasma cells, T cells, and perivascular cuffing.

Obtain a brain and orbits MRI with gadolinium for first episodes to assist with treatment and prognosis. C

Differential.Differential_Name: A tumor of the anterior visual pathway
Differential.Differential_Features: No pain with eye movement, usually insidious onset.

list.listitem: Optic neuritis should be suspected when a young patient (20-45 years old) complains of monocular or binocular vision loss, pain with eye movements, and loss of color vision. Patients are usually female (77%), Caucasian (8 times more likely), and often otherwise healthy. It is more commonly unilateral than bilateral.

The patient may have neurologic signs such as weakness, numbness, or tingling in the extremities. A relative afferent pupillary defect is present in unilateral or asymmetric cases (i.e. the direct pupillary light reflex is weaker and slower in the affected eye).
Optic neuritis may be preceded by flulike symptoms. Optic nerves welling will be present on fundoscopic exam in 33% of cases (67% are retrobulbar).
The Pulfrich phenomenon in patients with optic neuritis is when an object swinging to and fro is perceived as moving in a circular pattern.
Obtain an MRI with gadolinium of the brain and orbits to assess for areas of demyelination.
A meta-analysis of 11 studies concluded that MRI has 84% sensitivity and 86% specificity for diagnosis of optic neuritis (LR+ 6, LR- 0.15).
Patients with no lesions on MRI have a 22% risk of multiple sclerosis (MS) within 10 years.
Patients with 1 or more lesions on MRI have a 56% risk of multiple sclerosis within 10 years.

Among patients with acute optic neuritis, elevated levels of several spinal fluid biomarkers (TNF-alpha, IL-10, CXCL13 and NF-L) were associated with an increased likelihood of being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in the next 2 years.
If MS is suspected, consider blood tests to evaluate for other conditions such as Lyme disease, collagen vascular disease, and vitamin B12 deficiency.
Suspect optic neuritis in a young patient (especially a white female) with visual loss, pain with eye movements, and loss of color vision.
Look for a relative afferent pupillary defect.
MRI is the preferred imaging study to assess for multiple sclerosis.

If the brain and orbits MRI shows 1 or more areas of demyelination, start methylprednisone IV 1 g/day x3 days, followed by prednisone orally 1 mg/kg/day x11 days, then oral prednisone taper x4 days. This should be done within 2 weeks. A
If the brain and orbits MRI shows no lesions, the risk of multiple sclerosis is low, but pulsed IV steroids may hasten visual recovery. C
If the MRI shows 2 or more demyelinating lesions, refer to a neurologist for treatment with interferon-β-1a within 28 days. A

Methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg/day for 3 to 5 days has been previously recommended by some guidelines, but is somewhat controversial. A Cochrane systematic review found no evidence of long-term benefit of steroids for visual acuity, visual field, or contrast sensitivity.Although the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) found that a course of IV steroids given at the time of acute optic neuritis reduced the rate of development of clinically definite multiple sclerosis in the first 2 years, this effect disappears after 3 years. The ONTT also found that IV steroids increased the rate of vision recovery, although final visual acuity is the same in all groups. Oral steroid therapy alone increased the rate of recurrent optic neuritis, and this continued to be observed at the 5-year follow-up, although the mechanism has yet to be elucidated.
An analysis of 6 studies concluded that oral methylprednisolone is non-inferior to IV methylprednisolone.
A network meta-analysis of studies of treatment of neuromyelitis optica concluded that rituximab, azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil were the preferred first line therapies.
A network meta-analysis of 8 studies of patients with neuromyelitis optica concluded that ravulizumab was most likely to be successful at increasing time to relapse.

Data are limited for the addition of plasmapheresis or IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) to corticosteroids. A network meta-analysis identified 6 comparative studies with only 209 patients. The results suggest with low confidence that adding IVIG or plasmapheresis may improve the likelihood of visual recovery after an acute episode.
A retrospective cohort study found no advantage to treatment for 7 days with methylprednisolone over 5 days.

If the brain and orbits MRI shows 1 or more areas of demyelination, start methylprednisone IV 1 g/day x3 days, followed by prednisone orally 1 mg/kg/day x 11 days, and then oral prednisone taper x4 days. This should be done within 2 weeks. If the brain and orbits MRI shows no lesions, the risk of multiple sclerosis is low, but pulsed IV steroids may hasten visual recovery.
Atacicept is not effective based on a systematic review.
A randomized trial compared erythropoietin (EPO) with placebo in 108 patients with optic neuritis, and found no difference in visual outcomes or the likelihood of conversion to multiple sclerosis.
A meta-analysis identified 5 studies of various vitamins for patients with optic neuritis, but found no benefit.
If the MRI shows 2 or more demyelinating lesions, refer to a neurologist for treatment with interferon-β-1a within 28 days.

Treatment with interferon-β-1a showed a reduced risk of multiple sclerosis in the following 3 years (35% vs 50%, NNT = 6), along with a reduction in brain lesions. However, depression (NNH = 14) and flu-like symptoms (NNH = 4) were more common in the treatment group.
The initial visual defect resolves in over 90% of patients, but may recur.
Ten years following optic neuritis, visual acuity was better than 20/20 in 74% of eyes. B
Fifteen years following optic neuritis, visual acuity was better than 20/20 in 72% of eyes. B
Children with optic neuritis are at increased risk for developing MS, and this effect increases with age. Children with abnormal MRI scans are at substantially higher risk.
Data are limited but visual outcomes appear to be worse in optic neuritis following COVID-19 infection compared with optic neuritis following vaccination.
